pos: n. (one who shaves the head and beard; in Ezekiel, the razor is a sign of the coming siege)
etymology: From Old French barbeor, from Latin barba, a beard. The AV uses the word once, at Ezekiel 5:1, where the prophet is told to take a barber's razor to his own head and beard.
biblical_def:
Ezekiel's commissions are acted rather than spoken, and this is among the strangest of them: And thou, son of man, take thee a sharp knife, take thee a barber's razor, and cause it to pass upon thine head and upon thy beard: then take thee balances to weigh, and divide the hair. The prophet is made into the sign. His own hair is Jerusalem, and the three portions weighed out on the balances are the three ends of the city — a third burned in the midst when the siege is fulfilled, a third smitten with the knife, a third scattered in the wind with a sword drawn out after it.

The horror of the sign depends entirely on what a beard meant in Israel. The priests were forbidden to shave off the corner of the beard or make baldness upon their head; the Nazarite let no razor come upon his head at all for the days of his separation; and when Hanun shaved off half the beards of David's servants it was an act of war. For a priest of the LORD — Ezekiel was one — to take a barber's razor to his own head in public was to enact the stripping of everything that marked Israel as holy and set apart. A barber is an ordinary tradesman. That is the point. The instrument of the judgment was not a sword out of heaven but the commonest blade in the city, applied by a man to himself, in the sight of the people who were about to lose everything the hair stood for.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one whose occupation is to shave men, or to dress and trim their hair.
webster_full: BARBER, n. One whose occupation is to shave men, or to shave and dress hair.
RAZOR, n. An instrument for shaving off beard or hair.
BEARD, n. The hair that grows on the chin, lips and adjacent parts of the face, chiefly of male adults.
BALDNESS, n. The want of hair on the top of the head; loss of hair.
BALANCE, n. A pair of scales, for ascertaining the weight of bodies.
scriptures: Ezekiel 5:1
And thou, son of man, take thee a sharp knife, take thee a barber's razor, and cause it to pass upon thine head and upon thy beard: then take thee balances to weigh, and divide the hair.
Ezekiel 5:2

Thou shalt burn with fire a third part in the midst of the city, when the days of the siege are fulfilled: and thou shalt take a third part, and smite about it with a knife: and a third part thou shalt scatter in the wind; and I will draw out a sword after them.
Leviticus 21:5
They shall not make baldness upon their head, neither shall they shave off the corner of their beard, nor make any cuttings in their flesh.
Numbers 6:5

All the days of the vow of his separation there shall no razor come upon his head: until the days be fulfilled, in the which he separateth himself unto the LORD, he shall be holy, and shall let the locks of the hair of his head grow.
corruption_summary: The prophetic sign-acts are read as theatre or as symptoms rather than as commanded obedience, and the cost to the man who performed them disappears.
corruption_paragraphs: A reading now common treats Ezekiel's sign-acts — the shaved head, the tile, the four hundred and thirty days on his side, the untouched tears at his wife's death — as evidence of the prophet's psychological state rather than as obedience to explicit commands. The text will not support it. Every one of them is introduced by a direct word from the LORD and interpreted immediately afterward by the LORD, and the prophet's own reaction is recorded when he has one. To file the barber's razor under pathology is to lose the whole point of the office: God made the messenger into the message, and the messenger bore it.

The second loss is the weight of the sign for a priest. Ezekiel was of the priestly line and knew Leviticus 21 by heart. To put a razor to his head was to do in public the thing his order was forbidden to do, and to do it as a picture of what was about to happen to the holy city. The principle to recover is that God's servants have been asked for costly obedience in the currency they value most — Abraham the son, Hosea the marriage, Ezekiel the beard — and none of them was told to do it for effect. They were told to do it because the word was true and the people would not hear it spoken.
roots_summary: Hebrew gallab (H1532), a barber; taar (H8593), a razor; zaqan (H2206), the beard.
roots_lines: Hebrew gallab (H1532) — a barber; used once in the Old Testament, in Ezekiel's sign-act.
Hebrew taar (H8593) — a razor, from a root meaning to lay bare; the same word forbidden to the Nazarite.
Hebrew zaqan (H2206) — the beard; the mark of a man's dignity, and in Israel of his consecration.
Hebrew mozen (H3976) — a balance, scales; on which the hair of the city was weighed into thirds.

“there shall no razor come upon his head” — what the sign-act deliberately violated.

pos: v.t. (to work a pattern into cloth with the needle; used of the priest's coat of fine linen)
etymology: From Old French embroder, from brod, an embroidery or edge. At Exodus 28:39 it renders Hebrew shabats, to weave in checker work or to set in ouches — the same root used of stones set in gold.
biblical_def:
The instructions for the high priest's garments run for a whole chapter, and this is the last of them: And thou shalt embroider the coat of fine linen, and thou shalt make the mitre of fine linen, and thou shalt make the girdle of needlework. The coat was the innermost garment, worn under the robe and the ephod and the breastplate, and it was still to be embroidered — worked in checker, patterned throughout. Almost none of it would be seen. God commanded it anyway, and the command is one of Scripture's plainest statements about craftsmanship: the quality of a thing made for God is not measured by how much of it the congregation can see.

The workmen are named and their qualification is stated with unusual directness. Them hath he filled with wisdom of heart, to work all manner of work, of the engraver, and of the cunning workman, and of the embroiderer, in blue, and in purple, in scarlet, and in fine linen, and of the weaver. Bezaleel and Aholiab are the first men in Scripture said to be filled with the Spirit of God, and the filling is for metalwork, carpentry, stone-cutting, weaving, and the needle. That is a doctrine of vocation stated before the tabernacle stood: the Holy Ghost is credited, by name, with the skill of a man's hands, and the first recorded gifting of the Spirit in the Bible is given to artisans.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to border with ornamental needlework; to adorn with figures wrought with the needle.
webster_full: EMBROIDER, v.t. To border with ornamental needle-work, or figures; to adorn with raised figures of needle-work.
EMBROIDERY, n. Work in gold, silver or silk thread, formed by the needle on cloth or stuffs into various figures.
NEEDLEWORK, n. Work executed with a needle; the business of a seamstress.
MITRE, n. A sacerdotal ornament worn on the head by bishops and certain abbots; the head-dress of the Jewish high priest.
GIRDLE, n. A band or belt; something drawn round the waist of a person, and tied or buckled.
scriptures: Exodus 28:39
And thou shalt embroider the coat of fine linen, and thou shalt make the mitre of fine linen, and thou shalt make the girdle of needlework.
Exodus 35:35

Them hath he filled with wisdom of heart, to work all manner of work, of the engraver, and of the cunning workman, and of the embroiderer, in blue, and in purple, in scarlet, and in fine linen, and of the weaver, even of them that do any work, and of those that devise cunning work.
Exodus 31:3
And I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship,
Exodus 26:36
And thou shalt make an hanging for the door of the tent, of blue, and purple, and scarlet, and fine twined linen, wrought with needlework.
corruption_summary: Craft is treated as a lower calling than ministry, and Exodus 31 — the first filling with the Spirit in Scripture, given to a metalworker and an embroiderer — is read past.
corruption_paragraphs: Evangelical instinct still ranks callings, with the pulpit at the top and the workbench somewhere below, and a great many Christians in the trades have been quietly taught that their work is what pays for the real work. Exodus says otherwise and says it first. The earliest man in the Bible described as filled with the Spirit of God is Bezaleel, and the filling is itemized: wisdom, understanding, knowledge, and all manner of workmanship — gold, silver, brass, stone-cutting, timber, and, through Aholiab, the needle. The Reformers recovered this under the doctrine of vocation, and the confessional tradition has never had room for the two-tier reading.

The second thing to recover is the embroidered coat itself. It went on next to the skin, under three other garments, and was worked all over in checker. Nobody would see it but the priest and God. A generation of Christian work trained on metrics and audiences has trouble with that verse, because it commands excellence in a place where excellence can never be credited. It is the same principle that puts the cherubim on the inner walls of the house behind the gold, and the same one that governs the believer's hidden life: let it be the hidden man of the heart... which is in the sight of God of great price.

roots_lines: Hebrew shabats (H7660) — to set in checker work; the verb rendered embroider at Exodus 28:39.

Hebrew roqem (H7551) — the embroiderer; one of the three crafts named in Exodus 35:35.
Hebrew choshev (H2803) — the cunning workman, the deviser; the highest of the tabernacle crafts.

“Them hath he filled with wisdom of heart” — the Spirit credited with skill.
“the engraver, and... the cunning workman, and... the embroiderer” — three trades named in one breath.

pos: n. pl. (figures cut in wood; the cherubim, palm trees and open flowers of Solomon's house)
etymology: From Old English ceorfan, to cut. At 1 Kings 6:32 it renders Hebrew miqlaath, carved work, from qala, to carve or engrave — a word used only of the temple's interior.
biblical_def:
The account of Solomon's house slows almost to a standstill over its interior: The two doors also were of olive tree; and he carved upon them carvings of cherubims and palm trees and open flowers, and overlaid them with gold, and spread gold upon the cherubims, and upon the palm trees. Three figures are repeated everywhere in the house — cherubim, palm trees, open flowers — and then the whole thing is covered in gold. The carvings were not display. They went under the overlay.

The three figures are a garden. Cherubim guarded the way to the tree of life when man was driven out of Eden; palms and opening flowers are what a well-watered garden looks like; and the man who went in through those doors was walking back toward the place the flaming sword had closed. The second commandment was not being broken, because these were made by God's own command, and none of them was worshipped; Israel's sin was never in having carved cherubim over the mercy seat but in bowing to a calf. The mourning of Psalm 74 is the exact reverse of the making: But now they break down the carved work thereof at once with axes and hammers. What took seven years of patient cutting was undone in an afternoon, and the psalmist sets the two speeds side by side because the contrast is the grief.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): figures cut or engraved; the works of a carver in wood or stone.
webster_full: CARVING, n. The act or art of cutting figures in wood or stone; sculpture; figures carved.
CARVE, v.t. To cut, as wood, stone or other material, into some particular form; to engrave; to cut figures.
CHERUB, n. A figure composed of various creatures, as a man, an ox, an eagle or lion; two cherubs were placed on the mercy seat.
OVERLAY, v.t. To spread over; to cover the surface; to cover with a layer of metal.
PALM, n. The name of many species of trees; the branches were borne in token of victory.
scriptures: 1 Kings 6:32

The two doors also were of olive tree; and he carved upon them carvings of cherubims and palm trees and open flowers, and overlaid them with gold, and spread gold upon the cherubims, and upon the palm trees.
1 Kings 6:18
And the cedar of the house within was carved with knops and open flowers: all was cedar; there was no stone seen.
Psalm 74:6
But now they break down the carved work thereof at once with axes and hammers.
1 Kings 6:7

And the house, when it was in building, was built of stone made ready before it was brought thither: so that there was neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron heard in the house, while it was in building.
corruption_summary: The temple carvings are cited to justify images in worship, though every one of them was commanded by God, none was ever bowed to, and the house they filled was a type that ended at the torn veil.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome and the East both appeal to Solomon's cherubim and palm trees against the Reformed reading of the second commandment, and the appeal fails on three counts. First, every figure in the house was made by express divine command, which is precisely what the regulative principle requires and what a devotional image lacks. Second, no Israelite ever venerated them; the cherubim stood behind a veil that only one man passed, once a year, with blood. Third, the whole house was a shadow, and when the veil was rent from the top the shadow ended. The New Testament church is given no sanctuary furniture, no images, and no priesthood but Christ's.

The second corruption runs the other way. Some Reformed instinct has drifted from rejecting images in worship to suspecting beauty in general, as though bare walls were a virtue rather than a consequence. Solomon's house says otherwise: olive-wood doors, cedar carved with knops and open flowers, cherubim and palms in every room, and gold over all of it. What Scripture forbids is the image as a medium of worship, not skill, colour, or craft. A congregation may build well and beautifully; it may not build a thing to bow to.

“all was cedar; there was no stone seen” — the interior finished to the last surface.

pos: n. pl. (engraved work; the cut borders on the bases of the lavers in Solomon's house)
etymology: From Old English grafan, to dig or carve. At 1 Kings 7:31 it renders Hebrew miqlaoth, engravings; the related noun pittuach is used of the engravings of a signet on the priestly stones.
biblical_def:
The description of the ten brazen bases in Solomon's court is one of the most technical passages in Scripture, and it does not skip the underside of the work: and also upon the mouth of it were gravings with their borders, foursquare, not round. These were wheeled stands holding lavers for washing the instruments of sacrifice — utility furniture, standing in the open court, and engraved. Two verses later the record adds cherubim, lions and palm trees graved on the plates and ledges of the same bases, according to the proportion of every one. The Holy Ghost saw fit to preserve the fact that the washstands were beautiful.

The same craft appears in the holiest place the trade could reach. The onyx stones on the high priest's shoulders bore the names of the tribes cut like the engravings of a signet, and the golden plate on his forehead carried two words in the same hand: HOLINESS TO THE LORD. That is what engraving is for in Scripture — permanence. A signet cuts a name into metal so that what is stamped with it cannot be disputed, and the priest went in with the tribes cut into stone on his shoulders and the LORD's holiness cut into gold on his head. When Isaiah wants the strongest possible word for God's memory of His people, he reaches for the same craft: Behold, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): engravings; figures or letters cut into a hard surface with a sharp instrument.
webster_full: GRAVING, n. The act of carving or cutting figures; carved work; engraving.
GRAVE, v.t. To carve or cut letters or figures on stone or other hard substance; to engrave.
ENGRAVING, n. The act or art of cutting figures or letters on wood, stone or metal.
SIGNET, n. A seal; particularly, a seal used to give authority to a writing.
LAVER, n. A vessel for washing; a large basin used in the temple service.
scriptures: 1 Kings 7:31

And the mouth of it within the chapiter and above was a cubit: but the mouth thereof was round after the work of the base, a cubit and an half: and also upon the mouth of it were gravings with their borders, foursquare, not round.
1 Kings 7:36
For on the plates of the ledges thereof, and on the borders thereof, he graved cherubims, lions, and palm trees, according to the proportion of every one, and additions round about.
Exodus 28:11
With the work of an engraver in stone, like the engravings of a signet, shalt thou engrave the two stones with the names of the children of Israel: thou shalt make them to be set in ouches of gold.
Exodus 39:30
And they made the plate of the holy crown of pure gold, and wrote upon it a writing, like to the engravings of a signet, HOLINESS TO THE LORD.
corruption_summary: The long technical passages about the temple furniture are skipped as tedious, and with them goes the doctrine that God is particular about how His house is made.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Kings 7 is where a great many Bible-reading plans quietly lose their readers, and the loss is not neutral. The chapter exists to record that God specified the dimensions, the metals, the proportion and the ornament of vessels used for washing, and that He preserved the record afterward. That is the regulative principle in narrative form: the house of God is built to His word and not to the builder's taste, down to whether the mouth of a base is foursquare or round. A congregation that has never read the chapter will find it hard to see why Scripture must govern worship in the New Testament too.

There is no significant postmodern redefinition of this word to rebut. The principle to recover is the one the engraver's craft exists to teach: what is cut is permanent. The priest bore the names of the tribes cut into onyx on his shoulders whenever he went in, and Isaiah takes the same trade to make the strongest promise in the prophets — I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands; thy walls are continually before me. An engraving cannot be wiped off. That is why the Holy Ghost chose it for the doctrine of God's remembrance of His elect.

“HOLINESS TO THE LORD” — two words cut in gold on the priest's forehead.

pos: adj. (polished to a shine by friction; of the brass the living creatures' feet were like)
etymology: From Old French burnir, to make brown or bright by rubbing. At Ezekiel 1:7 it renders a Hebrew word from qalal, to be light or swift, used of brass made to gleam — polished, not merely cast.
biblical_def:
Ezekiel is describing the living creatures at the opening of his vision, and when he comes to their feet he reaches for the brightest thing a metalworker could produce: And their feet were straight feet; and the sole of their feet was like the sole of a calf's foot: and they sparkled like the colour of burnished brass. Burnished brass is brass that has been worked after casting, rubbed until it throws light. It is not a natural finish; somebody made it. The prophet has no other vocabulary for what he is seeing than the trades he grew up around, and this is how the whole vision proceeds — beryl, sapphire, amber, the sound of great waters, the noise of an host.

The same metal recurs at every appearance of the glory. Daniel's man clothed in linen has arms and feet like in colour to polished brass; John's vision of the risen Christ has feet like unto fine brass, as if they burned in a furnace. Brass in the tabernacle was the metal of the altar and the laver, the metal that stood in the place of judgment and of washing, and feet of burnished brass on the One who walks among the candlesticks are feet that can stand in fire. The imagery is not decorative. When the Lord Jesus addresses the compromised church at Thyatira He identifies Himself by exactly this detail — who hath his feet like fine brass — before He says I will give unto every one of you according to your works.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): polished; made bright and glossy by rubbing or friction.
webster_full: BURNISHED, pp. Polished; made glossy or bright by friction.
BURNISH, v.t. To polish by friction; to make smooth, bright and glossy.
BRASS, n. An alloy of copper and zinc, of a yellow color; in Scripture, often copper or bronze.
POLISH, v.t. To make smooth and glossy, usually by friction; to remove roughness.
SPARKLE, v.i. To emit sparks; to shine, glitter or glisten.
scriptures: Ezekiel 1:7
And their feet were straight feet; and the sole of their feet was like the sole of a calf's foot: and they sparkled like the colour of burnished brass.
Daniel 10:6

His body also was like the beryl, and his face as the appearance of lightning, and his eyes as lamps of fire, and his arms and his feet like in colour to polished brass, and the voice of his words like the voice of a multitude.
Revelation 1:15
And his feet like unto fine brass, as if they burned in a furnace; and his voice as the sound of many waters.
1 Kings 7:36
For on the plates of the ledges thereof, and on the borders thereof, he graved cherubims, lions, and palm trees, according to the proportion of every one, and additions round about.
corruption_summary: The visionary chapters are read as symbols to be decoded rather than as a prophet honestly reporting what he saw, and the reverence drains out of them.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 1 attracts two bad readings. The first treats it as a puzzle with a key — each wheel and creature standing for a nation, a church age, or, in the popular literature, a machine. The second treats it as literary convention borrowed from Babylonian iconography. Both miss what the chapter is at pains to say about itself. The prophet writes in the language of likeness throughout: the appearance of, as it were, the likeness of, and at the end, the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD. Four layers of qualification before he will say the word glory. That is not a code. That is a man telling the truth about something that exceeded his vocabulary, and his response is recorded — he fell upon his face.

The principle to recover is the one burnished brass supplies. The metal had to be worked after it was cast before it would shine, and the Lord who walks among the candlesticks is described by it because His feet can stand in the furnace. Thyatira was a church that tolerated what it should have judged, and the Lord introduced Himself to it by His feet before He said a word about its works. A congregation that has lost the fear of God in reading Ezekiel 1 will not feel the force of that introduction in Revelation 2.

Hebrew nagah (H5051) — brightness; the light round about the throne in Ezekiel's vision.

“his feet like unto fine brass, as if they burned in a furnace” — feet that stand in fire.

pos: n. pl. (masons who dressed the temple stone to square; the men of Gebal in the margin)
etymology: English stone + squarer, one who squares. At 1 Kings 5:18 it renders a Hebrew word the margin reads as Giblites — the men of Gebal, the Phoenician city known for its masons.
biblical_def:
The verse is a labour roster: And Solomon's builders and Hiram's builders did hew them, and the stonesquarers: so they prepared timber and stones to build the house. Three crews — Israelite, Tyrian, and the stonesquarers, whom the Hebrew names as men of Gebal, the coastal city whose masons were famous. The temple was built by covenant people and hired foreigners working the same stone, and Scripture records it without embarrassment. God's house in Jerusalem went up with Phoenician cedar, Phoenician gold-work, and Phoenician masons squaring the blocks.

The reason their work mattered is given in the next chapter, in one of the quietest and most remarkable verses in the historical books: And the house, when it was in building, was built of stone made ready before it was brought thither: so that there was neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron heard in the house, while it was in building. Every stone was cut, measured and squared at the quarry, so that when it came up to the mount it went into its place in silence. All the noise happened out of sight. Peter takes the picture up and makes it doctrine: Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood. The dressing of a living stone happens in the quarry of this life, under providence, with hammer and axe and a good deal of noise; the fitting together is silent, and it is the Builder's work, not the stone's.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): those who square stones; masons who dress and fit stone for building.
webster_full: SQUARER, n. One who squares; one that reduces to a square form.
SQUARE, v.t. To form with four equal sides and four right angles; to reduce to a true and even surface.
MASON, n. A man whose occupation is to lay bricks and stones, or to construct the walls of buildings.
HEW, v.t. To cut with an axe or other like instrument; to chop; to shape by cutting.
QUARRY, n. A place, cavern or pit where stones are dug from the earth.
scriptures: 1 Kings 5:18
And Solomon's builders and Hiram's builders did hew them, and the stonesquarers: so they prepared timber and stones to build the house.
1 Kings 5:17
And the king commanded, and they brought great stones, costly stones, and hewed stones, to lay the foundation of the house.
1 Kings 6:7

And the house, when it was in building, was built of stone made ready before it was brought thither: so that there was neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron heard in the house, while it was in building.
1 Peter 2:5
Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ.
corruption_summary: Sanctification is expected to be quiet and pleasant, when Scripture's own picture of it is a quarry full of hammers and the silence coming only at the end.
corruption_paragraphs: A believer who has been taught that the Christian life should feel like the finished house will be bewildered by his own experience. 1 Kings 6:7 describes the silence on the mount; it says nothing about the quarry, where the same stones were struck, split, measured and squared with iron. Peter's lively stones deliberately joins the two: the church is the house, and the members are the blocks, and the dressing happens here. Affliction, discipline, and the ordinary grinding providences are the tools, and the doctrine of sanctification is that they are wielded by a Builder who has the finished house in view and has measured every face.

The second thing worth recovering is the roster itself. Solomon's builders, Hiram's builders, and the Giblite masons worked side by side on the temple, and the text does not apologize for the hired Gentiles. Common grace supplies real skill to men outside the covenant, and the church has never been obliged to pretend otherwise. What it may not do is let those men set the design. The pattern came from God through David; the Phoenicians squared stone to it. Skill is borrowed freely; the rule of the house is not.

Hebrew pasal (H6458) — to hew, to square; the verb of the mason's trade.
Hebrew maqqabah (H4717) — a hammer; the tool not heard in the house while it was building.
Greek lithos zon (G3037 / G2198) — a living stone; Peter's figure for the members of the spiritual house.
usage: “Solomon's builders and Hiram's builders did hew them, and the stonesquarers” — three crews, one house.
“neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron heard in the house” — all the noise happened elsewhere.
“as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house” — Peter takes the quarry into doctrine.

pos: n. pl. (a carpenter's tools for smoothing wood; in Isaiah 44, part of the idol-maker's kit)
etymology: From Latin planus, level or flat, through Old French plane. At Isaiah 44:13 it renders Hebrew maqtsuah, a scraping tool, from qatsa, to cut off — the AV's only use of the word.
biblical_def:
Isaiah's great satire on idolatry works by refusing to skip a single step of the manufacture: The carpenter stretcheth out his rule; he marketh it out with a line; he fitteth it with planes, and he marketh it out with the compass, and maketh it after the figure of a man, according to the beauty of a man; that it may remain in the house. Rule, line, planes, compass. The prophet makes you watch the whole shop. He has already shown the man planting the ash and waiting years for the rain to grow it; he will presently show him burning half of it to warm himself and bake his bread, and falling down before the other half saying Deliver me; for thou art my god.

No argument is offered against idolatry in the chapter, because none is needed. The satire is the argument. A god that has to be levelled with a plane and finished to the measure of a man's beauty is a god whose whole existence postdates the tools. Habakkuk puts the same thing in a single question: What profiteth the graven image that the maker thereof hath graven it... to make dumb idols? The maker trusts in the work of his own hands, which is to say he trusts himself with an extra step inserted to hide the fact. And the plane is in the story because Isaiah wants the craftsmanship admitted — the man is genuinely skilled, the finish is genuinely fine, and none of that makes the block anything other than the other half of his firewood.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): tools used by joiners for smoothing boards, by paring off shavings.
webster_full: PLANE, n. In joinery, an instrument for paring or smoothing boards or other work.
PLANE, v.t. To make smooth; to pare off the inequalities of the surface of a board.
CARPENTER, n. An artificer who works in timber; a framer and builder of houses and of ships.
COMPASS, n. An instrument for describing circles, measuring figures, etc., consisting of two pointed legs.
RULE, n. An instrument by which lines are drawn; a ruler; a measure.
scriptures: Isaiah 44:13

The carpenter stretcheth out his rule; he marketh it out with a line; he fitteth it with planes, and he marketh it out with the compass, and maketh it after the figure of a man, according to the beauty of a man; that it may remain in the house.
Isaiah 44:14
He heweth him down cedars, and taketh the cypress and the oak, which he strengtheneth for himself among the trees of the forest: he planteth an ash, and the rain doth nourish it.
Isaiah 44:17
And the residue thereof he maketh a god, even his graven image: he falleth down unto it, and worshippeth it, and prayeth unto it, and saith, Deliver me; for thou art my god.
Habakkuk 2:18
What profiteth the graven image that the maker thereof hath graven it; the molten image, and a teacher of lies, that the maker of his work trusteth therein, to make dumb idols?
corruption_summary: Idolatry is filed as an ancient problem about statues, when Isaiah's satire is aimed at the universal instinct to make a god one can finish, measure and keep in the house.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern readers grant Isaiah 44 easily because nobody they know carves an ash tree. That concession is exactly what the chapter is designed to prevent. The prophet is not describing a primitive error; he is describing an appetite, and the appetite survives every change of technology. A god fitted with planes is a god made to specification — after the figure of a man, according to the beauty of a man — a deity finished to the maker's taste, portable, housed, and under control. Calvin's verdict stands: the human heart is a perpetual factory of idols, and the factory does not close when the woodshop does.

The contemporary form is a god assembled from the attributes a man finds agreeable and planed smooth wherever Scripture is rough. He is loving but not holy; he forgives but does not judge; he affirms and never commands. That figure is cut to the beauty of a man as surely as Isaiah's was, and it will do exactly as much for its maker in the day of trouble. The remedy is the one the chapter itself supplies in the verses on either side of the satire: I am the first, and I am the last; and beside me there is no God — a God who declares Himself, who cannot be finished, and who was not made.

“after the figure of a man, according to the beauty of a man” — a god cut to taste.
“Deliver me; for thou art my god” — addressed to the other half of the firewood.

pos: n. (the braiding of the hair; in 1 Peter 3:3, the elaborate coiffure set against the hidden man of the heart)
etymology: From Old French pleit, a fold, from Latin plicare, to fold. At 1 Peter 3:3 it renders Greek emploke, a braiding or interweaving — the Roman matron's hair, worked with gold thread and pins.
biblical_def:
Peter is writing to wives, some of them married to unbelieving husbands, and the counsel turns on where a woman's power actually lies: Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel; But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price. The contrast is not between ugliness and beauty but between two kinds of adorning, one outward and perishable and the other hidden and incorruptible, and the apostle uses the language of the jeweller for the second: an ornament, of great price, in the sight of God.

The plaiting Peter names was not a simple braid. First-century women of rank wore the hair built up in towers, interwoven with gold thread, pearls and pins, the work of hours and of servants. Paul gives the same instruction to Timothy's church in almost the same words — not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array — and the common thread is cost and display, not grooming. Neither apostle forbids a woman to arrange her hair, any more than Peter forbids apparel in the same breath as gold. What is forbidden is that the adorning should be that: that a woman's standing should be built on what can be taken off at night.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): braiding; folding or interweaving, as of the hair.
webster_full: PLAITING, ppr. Folding; doubling; braiding; interweaving.
PLAIT, n. A fold; a doubling; also, a braid of hair or straw.
ADORNING, n. Ornament; decoration; that which decorates or embellishes.
MEEK, a. Mild of temper; soft; gentle; not easily provoked or irritated; yielding.
APPAREL, n. Clothing; vesture; garments; dress.
scriptures: 1 Peter 3:3
Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel;
1 Peter 3:4
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
1 Timothy 2:9
In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array;
Exodus 28:39
And thou shalt embroider the coat of fine linen, and thou shalt make the mitre of fine linen, and thou shalt make the girdle of needlework.
corruption_summary: The passage is read either as a prohibition on braids and jewellery or as a dead letter about ancient fashion; both readings skip the thing Peter actually commends and prices.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite mistakes attach to these verses. Some have made them a rule about hair and metal, producing a legalism Peter did not write — the same sentence forbids putting on of apparel, and nobody reads that as a prohibition on clothes. Others dismiss the passage as first-century fashion commentary with nothing to say now. Both evade the positive command, which is the substance of the paragraph: let it be the hidden man of the heart... even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit. That is not a lesser beauty offered as consolation. It is the one Peter says is incorruptible and is, in God's sight, of great price.

The live corruption is the market that has grown up in the space Peter is talking about. An industry now exists to persuade women that worth is a thing purchased, applied, and photographed, and it is sustained by making the purchase never quite sufficient. Against that, a meek and quiet spirit is not a recommendation to be timid — meekness in Scripture is strength under government, and Peter immediately names Sara as the example, a woman who called Abraham lord and was no one's doormat. What he offers is an adorning that does not have to be reapplied, cannot be lost with age, and is appraised by the only judge whose valuation lasts.
roots_summary: Greek emploke (G1708), a braiding of the hair; kosmos (G2889), adorning; praus (G4239), meek; hesuchios (G2272), quiet.
roots_lines: Greek emploke (G1708) — a braiding, an interweaving; used once, of the elaborate coiffure of Peter's day.
Greek kosmos (G2889) — an ordering, an adorning; the root of our word cosmetic, and here of both adornings.
Greek praus (G4239) — meek, gentle; the same adjective our Lord applies to Himself in Matthew 11:29.
Greek hesuchios (G2272) — quiet, tranquil; not silent, but undisturbed.

usage: “that outward adorning of plaiting the hair” — hours of work, and perishable.
“the hidden man of the heart... which is not corruptible” — the adorning that lasts.
“in the sight of God of great price” — the only appraisal that holds.

pos: n. (soldering; the joining of metal with a fusible alloy — the last step in making an idol)
etymology: An older English spelling of soldering, from Old French soudure, from Latin solidare, to make solid. At Isaiah 41:7 it renders Hebrew debeq, a joining or cleaving together.
biblical_def:
Isaiah 41 is a courtroom scene in which the LORD summons the nations to produce their gods, and He shows us instead the workshop where the gods are produced: So the carpenter encouraged the goldsmith, and he that smootheth with the hammer him that smote the anvil, saying, It is ready for the sodering: and he fastened it with nails, that it should not be moved. The verse is a masterpiece of contempt achieved entirely by reporting. Four tradesmen cheer each other along; the joint is called ready; and the last act of the makers is to nail the god down so it will not fall over.

The preceding verse makes the irony explicit: They helped every one his neighbour; and every one said to his brother, Be of good courage. The idol-makers must encourage each other because the thing they are making cannot encourage anyone. Every function a god is supposed to perform is being performed by the men in the shop — they hearten one another, they hold the work steady, they secure it against falling. The contrast in the chapter around it is total. Two verses earlier the LORD says to Israel, Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee. The idol must be fastened with nails that it be not moved; the LORD holds His people with the right hand of His righteousness.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the act of uniting metals by a fusible alloy; soldering.
webster_full: SOLDERING, ppr. Uniting metals by a metallic cement; mending; patching up.
SOLDER, n. A metallic cement, or a metal or metallic alloy used to unite other metallic substances.
ANVIL, n. An iron block with a smooth face, on which smiths hammer and shape their work.
GOLDSMITH, n. An artisan who manufactures vessels and ornaments of gold and silver.
FASTEN, v.t. To fix firmly; to make fast or close; to secure in place.
scriptures: Isaiah 41:7

So the carpenter encouraged the goldsmith, and he that smootheth with the hammer him that smote the anvil, saying, It is ready for the sodering: and he fastened it with nails, that it should not be moved.
Isaiah 41:6
They helped every one his neighbour; and every one said to his brother, Be of good courage.
Isaiah 44:17
And the residue thereof he maketh a god, even his graven image: he falleth down unto it, and worshippeth it, and prayeth unto it, and saith, Deliver me; for thou art my god.
Habakkuk 2:18
What profiteth the graven image that the maker thereof hath graven it; the molten image, and a teacher of lies, that the maker of his work trusteth therein, to make dumb idols?
corruption_summary: Idolatry is imagined as belief in a statue, when Isaiah shows it as a social project — men encouraging one another around a thing they all know they made.
corruption_paragraphs: The workshop in Isaiah 41 is a picture of manufactured consensus. Nobody in that shop is deceived about where the god came from; they watched it being hammered. What holds the whole thing up is that they say Be of good courage to each other while they work. This is the social mechanism of every idolatry, including the modern varieties: what makes a thing credible is not evidence but the fact that everyone in the shop is nodding, and the nodding has to be constantly maintained because the object cannot maintain itself. Habakkuk names the idol a teacher of lies, and this is the lesson it teaches — that a thing enough people affirm together must be real.

The believer's protection is not scepticism but the contrast the chapter itself draws. The idol must be nailed down that it be not moved; the LORD says to His servant, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness. One is secured by its makers; the other secures His people. Where a Christian finds himself needing constant reassurance from others that a thing is so, it is worth asking which side of Isaiah 41 he is standing on — the shop where the courage is passed around, or the covenant where it is given from outside.

“They helped every one his neighbour” — the courage the idol could not supply.

pos: n. pl. (men who tread grapes in the winepress; in Isaiah 16, their shouting is silenced by judgment)
etymology: From Old English tredan, to tread. At Isaiah 16:10 it renders a Hebrew participle from darak, to tread — the same verb used of treading a bow and of treading the winepress in judgment.
biblical_def:
Isaiah's burden against Moab reaches its saddest line in the vineyards: And gladness is taken away, and joy out of the plentiful field; and in the vineyards there shall be no singing, neither shall there be shouting: the treaders shall tread out no wine in their presses; I have made their vintage shouting to cease. The vintage was the loudest, gladdest work of the year — men in the press to the knees, calling and singing as they trod, the noise carrying across the terraces. Judgment does not come to Moab as fire in this verse. It comes as silence where there should be shouting, and the LORD takes the credit for it in the first person: I have made their vintage shouting to cease. Jeremiah repeats the oracle almost word for word a century later.

The winepress becomes one of Scripture's great figures of wrath precisely because of how the work looks. Isaiah 63 has the LORD coming from Edom with dyed garments: I have trodden the winepress alone; and of the people there was none with me. John sees the same press outside the city, trodden until blood comes out to the horse bridles. And Amos reverses the whole picture for the day of restoration, when the treader of grapes overtakes the sower and the mountains drop sweet wine — the harvests running into each other so fast that the vintage never stops. The treaders are silenced in judgment and set singing again in mercy, and in between, One trod the press alone.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): those who tread; particularly, those who tread grapes in the wine-press.
webster_full: TREADER, n. One who treads; one who presses grapes in the vat.
TREAD, v.t. To press under the foot; to trample; to crush by the feet.
WINEPRESS, n. A vat or vessel in which grapes are pressed, to extract the juice.
VINTAGE, n. The produce of the vine for the season; the time of gathering the crop of grapes.
SHOUTING, n. The act of shouting; a loud cry of joy, exultation or triumph.
scriptures: Isaiah 16:10

And gladness is taken away, and joy out of the plentiful field; and in the vineyards there shall be no singing, neither shall there be shouting: the treaders shall tread out no wine in their presses; I have made their vintage shouting to cease.
Jeremiah 48:33

And joy and gladness is taken from the plentiful field, and from the land of Moab; and I have caused wine to fail from the winepresses: none shall tread with shouting; their shouting shall be no shouting.
Isaiah 63:3

I have trodden the winepress alone; and of the people there was none with me: for I will tread them in mine anger, and trample them in my fury; and their blood shall be sprinkled upon my garments, and I will stain all my raiment.
Amos 9:13

Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that the plowman shall overtake the reaper, and the treader of grapes him that soweth seed; and the mountains shall drop sweet wine, and all the hills shall melt.
corruption_summary: The winepress of wrath is the passage most often quietly dropped, and a gospel that has lost it has lost the reason the cross was necessary.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 63 is a text modern preaching finds hard to say aloud: a figure coming from Edom with garments dyed red, treading the press alone, staining all His raiment. The instinct to soften it usually takes one of two forms — reading the wrath as impersonal consequence, or restricting it to the Old Testament and leaving it behind. Neither survives contact with Revelation 14, where the press is trodden outside the city, or with Romans, where the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness. Strip the winepress out and the atonement becomes a demonstration of love with nothing to save anyone from.

Held together, the images preach the gospel by themselves. The treaders of Moab fall silent under judgment. The LORD treads the press alone, with none of the people with Him — which is exactly what Gethsemane and Golgotha looked like from the inside. And Amos ends with the vintage that never stops, the plowman overtaking the reaper, the mountains dropping sweet wine. The silence, the solitary treading, and the shouting restored are three views of one work, and the middle one is why the third is possible.
